questions.q: In the generic router architecture, which component makes up the control plane?
choices: The high-speed switching fabric
The input ports
The routing processor
The output ports
questions.explain: The routing processor runs routing and management, which is the control plane (software). The input ports, switching fabric and output ports together form the forwarding data plane.

questions.q: Which description fits a router's forwarding data plane?
choices: Implemented in software, operates in a millisecond time frame
Implemented in hardware, operates in a nanosecond time frame
Implemented in software, operates in a nanosecond time frame
Implemented in hardware, operates in a millisecond time frame
questions.explain: Forwarding happens for every datagram, so it is done in hardware on a nanosecond time scale. The control plane (routing, management) is software working on a millisecond time scale.

questions.q: Which of these are part of a router's forwarding data plane?
choices: Input ports
Routing processor
High-speed switching fabric
Output ports
Routing and management software
questions.explain: Input ports, the switching fabric and output ports move datagrams, so they make up the data plane. The routing processor and its routing and management software make up the control plane.

questions.q: The router's routing and management functions work on a much slower time scale than forwarding individual datagrams.
questions.explain: The control plane (routing, management) works in milliseconds. The forwarding data plane must handle each datagram in nanoseconds.

questions.q: In the generic router architecture, which path does an arriving datagram take?
choices: Input port → routing processor → output port
Routing processor → switching fabric → input port
Output port → switching fabric → input port
Input port → switching fabric → output port
questions.explain: Datagrams enter at an input port, cross the high-speed switching fabric, and leave through an output port. The routing processor sits above the fabric in the control plane and is not on the datagram's path.

questions.q: In what order does an input port process an arriving datagram before it reaches the switch fabric?
choices: Line termination → link-layer protocol (receive) → lookup, forwarding, queueing
Link-layer protocol (receive) → line termination → lookup, forwarding, queueing
Lookup, forwarding, queueing → line termination → link-layer protocol (receive)
Line termination → lookup, forwarding, queueing → link-layer protocol (receive)
questions.explain: Bits are received first (line termination, physical layer), then the link-layer protocol (e.g., Ethernet) handles the frame, then lookup/forwarding/queueing sends the datagram into the switch fabric.

questions.q: What does the line termination stage of an input port do?
choices: Runs the link-layer protocol, such as Ethernet
Bit-level reception at the physical layer
Looks up the output port in the forwarding table
Computes routes with other routers
questions.explain: Line termination is the physical layer: bit-level reception. The link-layer protocol stage comes next, followed by lookup/forwarding/queueing.

questions.q: An input port uses header field values to find the output port in its forwarding table. This style of processing is described as "match plus ____".
questions.explain: "Match plus action": the header fields are matched against the forwarding table, and the matching entry says what to do, such as which output port to forward to.

questions.q: Why is the lookup at the input port called decentralized switching?
choices: Lookups are spread across several routers along the path
The routing processor performs every lookup for all ports
Each input port finds the output port itself, using a forwarding table held in the input port's memory
The switching fabric chooses the output port while the datagram is in transit
questions.explain: Each input port has the forwarding table in its own memory and does the lookup locally, so no central processor has to handle every datagram.

questions.q: When does queueing happen at an input port?
choices: When the routing processor is recomputing routes
When datagrams arrive faster than they can be forwarded into the switch fabric
Only when the forwarding table has no matching entry
When the forwarding table is being copied to the output ports
questions.explain: Input port queuing occurs if datagrams arrive faster than the forwarding rate into the switch fabric, so they wait at the input.

questions.q: The goal for input port processing is to finish at 'line speed', that is, to keep up with the rate at which datagrams arrive on the input link.
questions.explain: If lookup and forwarding can't keep up with line speed, datagrams pile up in the input port's queue.

questions.q: A router chooses the output port using only the datagram's destination IP address. What is this called?
choices: Generalized forwarding
Switching via memory
Destination-based forwarding
Decentralized routing
questions.explain: Destination-based forwarding (the traditional approach) uses only the destination IP address. Generalized forwarding can use any set of header field values.

questions.q: Generalized forwarding chooses the output port based only on the destination IP address.
questions.explain: That describes destination-based forwarding. Generalized forwarding can forward based on any set of header field values.

choices: Interface 0
Interface 1
Interface 2
Interface 3
questions.explain: The third byte 00010110 begins with 00010, so the address matches the interface-0 prefix. It doesn't match 00011000 or 00011***, so that is the only (and longest) match.

choices: Interface 0
Interface 1
Interface 2
Interface 3
questions.explain: The address matches both 00011000 (interface 1, a 24-bit prefix) and 00011*** (interface 2, a 21-bit prefix). Longest prefix matching picks the longer one, interface 1.

choices: Interface 0
Interface 1
Interface 2
Interface 3
questions.explain: The third byte is 00011001, which is not 00011000, so the interface-1 entry fails. It does begin with 00011, so it matches the interface-2 entry.

choices: Interface 0
Interface 1
Interface 2
Interface 3
questions.explain: The first two bytes match, but the third byte begins 00001, which is neither 00010 nor 00011. No entry's full prefix matches, so the 'otherwise' entry (interface 3) applies.

questions.q: When several forwarding-table entries match a destination address, which one does longest prefix matching use?
choices: The entry listed first in the table
The entry with the shortest prefix, since it covers the most addresses
The entry for the least busy link interface
The entry with the longest prefix that matches the destination address
questions.explain: Longest prefix match: when looking up the forwarding-table entry for a destination address, use the longest address prefix that matches it.

questions.q: Destination 11001000 00010111 00011000 10101010 matches both 11001000 00010111 00011000 ******** (interface 1) and 11001000 00010111 00011*** ******** (interface 2). The router sends it to interface 2 because that entry covers more addresses.
questions.explain: The longer (more specific) prefix wins. 11001000 00010111 00011000 is 24 bits and 11001000 00010111 00011 is 21 bits, so the datagram goes to interface 1.

questions.q: How many bits long is the prefix in the forwarding-table entry 11001000 00010111 00010*** ******** (count the bits that are not wildcards)?
questions.explain: 8 bits + 8 bits + 5 bits (00010) = 21 bits. The remaining 11 bits are wildcards.

questions.q: How many different 32-bit destination addresses match the forwarding-table entry 11001000 00010111 00010*** ********?
questions.explain: 21 bits are fixed and 11 are wildcards, so 2^11 = 2048 addresses match. This is the range 11001000 00010111 00010000 00000000 through 11001000 00010111 00010111 11111111.

questions.q: A router sends 11001000 00010111 00010000 00000000 through 11001000 00010111 00010111 11111111 to interface 0. The four addresses 11001000 00010111 00010000 00000100 through 11001000 00010111 00010000 00000111 must go to interface 3 instead. How many bits long is the prefix of a single entry that covers exactly those four addresses?
questions.explain: The four addresses differ only in their last 2 bits (100, 101, 110, 111 → 000001**), so the entry is 11001000 00010111 00010000 000001**: 32 − 2 = 30 bits.

questions.q: A router sends 11001000 00010111 00010000 00000000 through 11001000 00010111 00010111 11111111 to interface 0, but the four addresses 11001000 00010111 00010000 00000100 through ...00000111 must go to interface 3. How does longest prefix matching handle this range that doesn't divide up nicely?
choices: Send those four addresses to the 'otherwise' entry
Have the routing processor forward those four addresses in software
Add an entry 11001000 00010111 00010000 000001** → interface 3; it is a longer match for those four addresses, while the shorter interface-0 prefix still handles the rest of the range
Split the interface-0 range into separate entries that skip those four addresses, because entries are not allowed to overlap
questions.explain: Entries may overlap. A destination in the small sub-range matches both entries, and the longer 30-bit prefix wins, so it goes to interface 3. All other addresses match only the 21-bit interface-0 prefix.

questions.q: Longest prefix matching is often done in hardware using TCAMs. What does TCAM stand for?
questions.explain: TCAM = ternary content addressable memory.

questions.q: What makes a content-addressable memory attractive for forwarding-table lookup?
choices: It searches the table one entry at a time, but in hardware rather than software
You present the address and it retrieves the matching entry in one clock cycle, regardless of table size
It compresses the table so it fits in the routing processor's cache
It lets the router skip lookup for destinations it has already seen
questions.explain: Content addressable: you present an address to the TCAM and it retrieves the result in one clock cycle, no matter how big the table is.

questions.q: With a TCAM, a lookup takes longer as the forwarding table grows from thousands of entries to around a million.
questions.explain: A TCAM lookup takes one clock cycle regardless of table size. For example, the Cisco Catalyst holds about 1M routing table entries in TCAM.

questions.q: Which forwarding operation are TCAMs often used to perform?
choices: Reassembling cells into datagrams
Bit-level reception on the input link
Longest prefix matching
Computing routes with other routers
questions.explain: Longest prefix matching is often performed using TCAMs, so the lookup finishes in one clock cycle.

questions.q: What is a switching fabric's switching rate?
choices: The rate at which bits arrive on a single input link
How often the routing processor updates the forwarding table
The rate at which packets can be transferred from inputs to outputs
The number of output ports the fabric connects to
questions.explain: The switching fabric moves packets from an input link to the right output link. Its switching rate is how fast it can move packets from inputs to outputs.

questions.q: A router has N = 8 input ports, each with line rate R = 10 Gbps. What switching rate (in Gbps) is ideally desirable for its fabric?
questions.explain: With N inputs, a switching rate of N times the line rate is desirable: N × R = 8 × 10 Gbps = 80 Gbps.

questions.q: Why is a switching rate of N times the line rate desirable for a router with N inputs?
choices: So the fabric can move traffic arriving at full line rate on all N inputs at the same time, without it backing up at the inputs
So each packet can cross the fabric N times for reliability
Because the control plane needs N times the bandwidth of the data plane
Because every datagram is split into N cells
questions.explain: Every input can receive at rate R at once, a total of NR. A fabric that switches at NR can keep up. A slower one makes datagrams queue at the input ports.

questions.q: Switching rate is often measured as a multiple of the input/output line rate.
questions.explain: For example, a fabric for N inputs at line rate R would ideally run at NR, which is N times the line rate.

questions.q: A switching fabric runs at 40 Gbps and each input link runs at 10 Gbps. For how many input ports is 40 Gbps exactly the ideal N × R switching rate?
questions.explain: N × R = 40 Gbps with R = 10 Gbps gives N = 4.

questions.q: Which are the three major types of switching fabrics?
choices: Memory
Bus
Interconnection network
Routing processor
TCAM
Line termination
questions.explain: The three major fabric types are switching via memory, via a bus, and via an interconnection network (e.g., crossbar).

questions.q: How did first-generation routers switch datagrams?
choices: Through a crossbar connecting each input to each output
They were traditional computers: under direct CPU control, each datagram was copied into system memory and then out to the output port
Over a shared bus straight from input port memory to output port memory, without involving the CPU
Through multiple switching planes working in parallel
questions.explain: First-generation routers switched via memory. They were ordinary computers in which the CPU copied each packet into system memory and then out to the output port.

questions.q: In switching via memory, why is speed limited by memory bandwidth?
choices: The forwarding table is too large to fit in system memory
Datagrams must first be split into fixed-length cells
Only one input port can send per clock cycle of the TCAM
Each datagram crosses the system bus twice: into memory from the input port, then out of memory to the output port
questions.explain: Every datagram crosses the bus twice, into and out of memory, so the shared memory and bus bandwidth caps forwarding speed.

questions.q: A router switches via memory, and its system bus can carry at most 20 Gbps. Ignoring other overhead, what is the most datagram traffic (in Gbps) it can forward from inputs to outputs?
questions.explain: Each datagram crosses the bus twice (input → memory, memory → output), so forwarded traffic is at most 20 / 2 = 10 Gbps.

questions.q: In switching via a bus, what limits switching speed?
choices: CPU speed, because the CPU copies every datagram into system memory
Bus bandwidth, because all datagrams compete for the one shared bus (bus contention)
The number of switching planes
The length of the fixed-size cells
questions.explain: Bus contention: every datagram must use the same shared bus, so switching speed is limited by the bus bandwidth.

questions.q: In switching via a bus, a datagram goes from input port memory to output port memory over a shared bus without first being copied into the system's main memory.
questions.explain: That is the difference from switching via memory, where the CPU copies each datagram into system memory (two bus crossings).

questions.q: A 32 Gbps bus-based fabric (as in the Cisco 5600) is described as fast enough for which kind of router?
choices: Access routers
Large routers needing hundreds of Tbps of switching capacity
Any router, regardless of how many ports it has or how fast they are
None; bus fabrics are too slow for any router
questions.explain: A 32 Gbps bus is enough for access routers. Routers needing much higher capacity use interconnection networks, e.g., the Cisco CRS with up to 100s of Tbps.

questions.q: Which of these are interconnection networks that can serve as a router's switching fabric?
choices: Crossbar
Shared bus
Clos network
System memory under CPU control
questions.explain: Crossbars, Clos networks and other interconnection networks are one fabric type. A shared bus and system memory are the other two fabric types.

questions.q: Interconnection networks such as crossbars and Clos networks were initially developed for what purpose?
choices: Connecting LANs to the Internet
Connecting processors in a multiprocessor
Storing forwarding tables for one-cycle lookup
Carrying Ethernet frames between routers
questions.explain: Crossbar, Clos and other interconnection networks were first developed to connect processors in multiprocessors, and were later used as router fabrics.

questions.q: What is a multistage switch?
choices: A switch that processes each datagram several times for reliability
A bus shared by several routers
An n×n switch built from multiple stages of smaller switches
A router with separate control and data planes
questions.explain: A multistage switch builds a large n×n switch out of stages of smaller switches, e.g., an 8x8 multistage switch built from smaller-sized switches.

questions.q: To exploit parallelism in an interconnection-network fabric, what happens to a datagram?
choices: It is copied into system memory and then out to the output port
It is copied to every output port and dropped wherever it isn't needed
It crosses the fabric as one unit through every stage at once
It is fragmented into fixed-length cells on entry, the cells are switched through the fabric, and the datagram is reassembled at exit
questions.explain: Splitting datagrams into fixed-length cells lets the fabric switch cells in parallel. The datagram is reassembled when it leaves the fabric.

questions.q: The cells a datagram is split into for switching through an interconnection network vary in length to fit the datagram.
questions.explain: The datagram is fragmented into fixed-length cells on entry and reassembled at the exit.

questions.q: How does a large router such as the Cisco CRS get speedup and scaleup in its switching fabric?
choices: By using multiple switching planes in parallel
By using one faster shared bus
By copying each datagram through system memory
By moving forwarding lookups to the routing processor
questions.explain: Scaling comes from running multiple switching 'planes' in parallel, which gives speedup and scaleup through parallelism.

questions.q: What is the basic unit of the Cisco CRS router's switching fabric?
choices: A single 3x3 crossbar
8 switching planes, each a 3-stage interconnection network
A 32 Gbps shared bus
8 CPUs, each copying datagrams through system memory
questions.explain: The Cisco CRS uses 8 switching planes as its basic unit. Each plane is a 3-stage interconnection network, giving up to 100s of Tbps of switching capacity.
